newsitem.title: UK: Major vows N.Ireland peace process will continue.
newsitem.headline: Major vows N.Ireland peace process will continue.

text.p: Prime Minister John Major described the IRA's admission to the bombing of British Army headquarters in Northern Ireland "as sickening hypocrisy" and vowed that it would not deflect the peace process.

He told reporters at the Conservative Party's last annual conference before the next election that Gerry Adams, leader of the political wing of the Irish Republican Army (IRA), had shown his true colours.
"So much of what Mr Adams...and the IRA have said in the last two years is nothing less than sickening hypocrisy," he said.

"Within the last few days Mr Adams has been asking to come and talk to me, asking to carry the peace process forward and all the time he knew they had planned to murder people in Lisburn. I hope people will see very clearly precisely what they are and treat their words for what they are worth."
Thirty-one people, including 20 soldiers, were injured in the twin car bombs on Monday afternoon within the perimeters of headquarters in Lisburn, near Belfast.

It was the first attack in the province by the IRA, which has waged a 25-year battle against British rule in Northern Ireland, since it broke a 17-month ceasefire in February, and the most serious setback to the struggling peace process since it began in 1993.
In a statement released later from his Downing Street office, Major said the search for a lasting peace in Northern Ireland would continue.

"I will not be deflected from the search for a political settlement to make possible a lasting peace. We will redouble our efforts at the multi-party talks. Sinn Fein have excluded themselves more clearly than ever."

The British leader said the provisional IRA was trying to provoke all-out war in the province and he urged Protestant loyalists, who support London's role in the province, not to break their ceasefire and revert to violence.

Sinn Fein has been barred from the all-party talks until it renews its truce. It refuses to accept any preconditions for inclusions in the peace process and has accused Major and his government of blocking chances for peace.
Major said the IRA's latest attack would open the eyes of some of its U.S. supporters who have previously backed the group.

"I think there is a much more balanced opinion in the U.S. I hope the people in the U.S. who were previously prepared to back the IRA with money will now realise they are backing people who are prepared to murder indiscriminately and in large numbers for a political purpose."
